definition: Arable means suitable for growing crops.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word arable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know arable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Less than a tenth of the mountain kingdom is arable, so every scrap of level ground has been terraced and planted for centuries.
Barren ground sits at the floor of this scale, far below arable: it answers every seed the same way — with nothing — while arable land can at least be plowed and planted.
Bountiful goes past arable — arable only promises that crops can grow; bountiful means the ground is already pouring out more than its people can store.

Farmable is the plain, everyday way to say it: this ground can be farmed. Arable is the surveyor's and geographer's term for the same judgment — land suitable for growing crops — the word that maps, ministries, and land registries reach for.

Plowable makes a narrower claim than arable: the blade can cut this ground, and that is all. Arable adds the judgment that matters — soil deep and sound enough for crops to grow once the plowing is done. A gravel flat may be plowable yet never arable.

Arable is the last common English trace of Latin arare, "to plow." The verb itself never made the crossing into English — even plow comes from a different, Germanic line — so arable stands alone, one word carrying a whole lost verb on its back.
Arable means suitable for growing crops.
In 1940 the ministry sent surveyors out with one question: what else can be plowed?
Golf links, deer parks, village greens — each was walked, augered, and judged.
Good depth of soil, drainage, a slope a tractor could hold: if the ground was arable, onto the list it went, and by spring the fairways were under wheat.
The blockade had turned a lazy word on old maps into the most urgent question in the country.
Arable is the exact word for what those surveyors were hunting, because it means suitable for growing crops — nothing more and nothing less.
It does not promise a good yield, and it says nothing about beauty or ownership; it draws the one line that mattered that year, between ground that can feed people and ground that cannot.
Arable is the surveyor's and geographer's word — arable land, arable acreage — and it draws a hard line: can crops grow here or not?
It says nothing about how much will grow; for that, reach for fertile or bountiful.

When the city inherited eight hundred vacant lots, the parks department assumed community gardens could bloom on all of them.
The soil survey said otherwise.
Decades of demolition had left most lots packed with brick dust, ash, and buried rubble.
Only ninety-one parcels were judged arable — dirt loose enough to work and clean enough to trust with food crops.
